questions.prompt: You have 2 buttons and get 3 more. How many are there altogether?
questions.explanation: Count the two buttons and the three new ones together. There are five.

questions.prompt: What does the + sign ask you to do here?
questions.explanation: Plus joins the amounts. Two piles become one total.

questions.prompt: You have 4 blocks and get 0 more. How many blocks do you have?
questions.explanation: Zero more means nothing was added. The original four blocks are still there.

title: What does adding actually mean?
practice: Ready for a faster challenge? Math Rush is optional; come back to these counters whenever you need them.

sections.html:
Put 2 buttons on a table. Beside them, put 3 more buttons. Now slide the two piles together.

Count every button once: one, two, three, four, five. You have 5 altogether. You have just added two amounts.

That is a good place to start with addition: finding how many there are when amounts are put together. You can use buttons, blocks or your fingers. There is no timer here.
sections.title: Two piles become one

sections.html:
Draw two circles on paper. Put two small objects inside one and three inside the other. Before counting, predict the total.

Move one object from the second circle to the first. You still have five, now arranged as three and two. Add a new object instead, and the total changes to six.
sections.title: Make a sum you can see

sections.html:
Instead of drawing all the buttons, we can write 2 + 3 = 5. Here is how to read it.

The signs in our button story
SignMeaning here
+ Plus: put the amounts together.
=Equals: both sides have the same amount.

Read the whole line as “two plus three equals five”. The answer to an addition is sometimes called the sum. Here, the sum is five.
sections.title: Those little signs tell the same story

sections.html:
Imagine you already counted 4 blocks. Someone gives you 2 more.

  1. Keep the first number, four, in your head.
  2. Count the first new block: five.
  3. Count the second new block: six.

You now have six blocks. We write that as 4 + 2 = 6. Counting every block from one would give the same answer.
sections.title: You do not always have to start at one

sections.html:
If you have 4 blocks and receive no extra blocks, you still have 4. Zero means none, so we can write 4 + 0 = 4.

Try this: put 3 counters beside 2 counters. Then swap the piles. You still have five. Moving the piles does not create or remove anything.

Next, we will do the opposite sort of story: take some things away and see what is left.

For the full picture, explore seven friendly starting points for basic arithmetic.
sections.title: What if nobody gives you any more?

description: Put two little piles together and count what you have. Try moving counters, learn what + and = mean, and build your first sums.
